title: A Request for Testosterone / Treat the Sleep Apnoea and the Driving First

blocks.text: A Request for Testosterone / Treat the Sleep Apnoea and the Driving First

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-29 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: Endocrine Society: Testosterone therapy in men with hypogonadism (Bhasin et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:1715-1744); DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025); GMC: Confidentiality, patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) · Related AMaC: AMaC obstructive sleep apnoea station; this one tests testosterone requests with contraindications

Dear Doctor, a 58-year-old company director. A private clinic found a low testosterone on one morning sample and advised testosterone. He is tired, has low libido and a BMI of 36. His GP notes severe obstructive sleep apnoea, for which he does not use his CPAP. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Tiredness and low libido in an obese man with untreated sleep apnoea has several treatable causes before testosterone. Check the contraindications, repeat the levels and deal with the risk of him falling asleep at the wheel.

The Examiner Trap. He wants testosterone, drives 90 minutes to work and dozes in traffic. Candidates write the prescription. Pass: repeat levels, contraindications, treat sleep apnoea, stop driving. Fail: testosterone prescribed, driving allowed.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 58-year-old company director. You are brisk, tired and used to getting what you ask for.
Opening line: "The clinic says my testosterone is low. I've got no energy and no drive. I just need the prescription."
Volunteered: the clinic took one blood test. They quoted a monthly price.
Only if asked: you stopped CPAP a year ago because the mask annoyed you. You doze in traffic jams on your 90-minute commute. You have not told anyone.

Only if asked about urination: you get up twice a night and the stream is weaker. No heart problems. No opioids. Background, only if asked: no regular medicines and no allergies. You do not smoke. You drink a few glasses of wine at weekends. No recent travel. No family history of note. You live with your wife.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of losing your edge and your business. Say: "If I can't drive, how do I get to work?"
Your questions, in your own words: "Why can't I have it?" "Is it dangerous?" "What about driving?"
How you react: if told no with no reason, you argue. If listened to and given a clear plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: BMI 36; thick neck; blood pressure 146/90; pulse 78 regular; temperature 36.6 °C. Mild breast enlargement. No oedema. Genital and rectal findings are not examined on the role-player: the examiner gives them only if the candidate asks, explains the indication, and says consent and a chaperone would be arranged. Testes normal in size. Prostate smooth, mildly enlarged.
Results, only when requested: repeat fasting morning testosterone: low-normal. LH and FSH inappropriately normal. Haematocrit 56%. PSA 4.6 ng/mL. Prolactin normal.

Question ladder: 1. Why not start testosterone now? (E, R5) One low level is not diagnostic, and a haematocrit of 56%, a PSA of 4.6 ng/mL and untreated severe sleep apnoea are contraindications. 2. Which results are contraindications? (E, R5) Raised haematocrit and PSA above 4 ng/mL without urology review. 3. How many testosterone levels are needed? (E, R5) Two fasting morning levels. 4. What are the driving rules? (E, R6) Moderate or severe sleep apnoea syndrome: he must not drive and must notify DVLA until controlled. 5. How would you monitor treatment later? (E, R6) Testosterone and haematocrit at 3 to 6 months, then annually.

Curveballs: He asks to carry on driving: no, moderate or severe sleep apnoea syndrome means he must not drive until it is controlled, and he must notify DVLA. He says the clinic can monitor him: monitoring needs a plan. He asks about the PSA: urology evaluation first.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Drop your trousers. [R1 Fail] How is your energy? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the blood pressure.) [R3 Fail] Low testosterone. [R4 Fail] No more tests. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: I'll prescribe testosterone, and you can keep driving. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a year. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): a man who dozes at the wheel with untreated severe sleep apnoea must not drive. No consent, no tests, and testosterone prescribed against contraindications.
Pass performance

CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your weight, blood pressure, neck and chest? Tell me if anything hurts. I'd also like to know the testicular and prostate findings, because they affect whether testosterone is safe; I'd ask your consent and have a chaperone. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Do you use your CPAP? Do you doze while driving? Any urinary symptoms? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: No CPAP. I doze in traffic. I get up twice at night.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, asks the examiner for the testicular findings, then covers him and thanks him.) A raised BMI, a thick neck, mild breast enlargement and, as given, normal-sized testes. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: One low level isn't enough, and your weight and sleep apnoea can lower testosterone. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I need two fasting morning levels, LH and FSH, a blood count, a PSA and prolactin. A thick blood count, high PSA and untreated sleep apnoea make testosterone unsafe now. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Please don't drive, and you must tell the DVLA yourself. If you carry on driving I may have to tell them, and I would warn you first. Restart CPAP and aim to lose weight. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: How I get to work.
CANDIDATE: That is fair; with your permission I can write a letter for you to give your employer, and we'll plan how you get to work. [R7 Pass] Shall we arrange CPAP support this week? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Refused testosterone safely and gave driving advice. Did not name other causes, the PSA threshold, monitoring or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? These symptoms are personal. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any stroke, clots or opioid use? What did the clinic tell you? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines; asks for the prostate findings.) As given, a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate; no oedema. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Opioids, illness and pituitary disease are other causes; LH and FSH help tell them apart. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: A haematocrit of 56%, a PSA above 4 ng/mL, untreated severe sleep apnoea and thrombophilia are contraindications, and the PSA needs urology review. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: If we start later, we'd check testosterone and haematocrit at 3 to 6 months and then yearly. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: We'll talk about your commute and your income. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a letter for the clinic. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, other causes, the thresholds, urology review, monitoring and a letter for the clinic.
R2: Not asking about CPAP and driving. Dozing at the wheel is the immediate danger.
R4: Accepting one low level. Two fasting morning levels, LH and FSH are needed.
R5: Ignoring the contraindications. A high haematocrit, a high PSA and untreated sleep apnoea all stop treatment.
R6: Prescribing and letting him drive. Both are unsafe.
"Can I ask whether you use your CPAP and how you cope on the drive?"
"One low level isn't enough; I'd like to repeat it."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

Endocrine Society 2018: contraindications to starting testosterone include breast or prostate cancer, a palpable prostate nodule, PSA above 4 ng/mL (3 in high-risk men) without urological evaluation, elevated haematocrit, untreated severe obstructive sleep apnoea, uncontrolled heart failure, myocardial infarction or stroke within the last 6 months, and thrombophilia.

Diagnose on symptoms plus two fasting morning total testosterone levels; look for reversible causes such as obesity, opioids and systemic illness. If treated: testosterone and haematocrit at 3 to 6 months, then 12 months and annually; hold treatment if haematocrit exceeds 54%. UK shared-care protocols may use a lower haematocrit threshold than the Endocrine Society's 54%, so follow the local protocol.

DVLA (last updated 7 November 2025): obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome of any severity counts as excessive sleepiness. With moderate (AHI 15 to 29) or severe (AHI 30 or more) apnoea the driver must not drive and must notify DVLA, and may be relicensed once the condition is controlled, sleepiness has improved and treatment adherence is confirmed (reviews at least every 3 years for Group 1 and annually for Group 2). With mild (AHI below 15) or suspected apnoea the driver must not drive until symptoms are controlled, and must notify DVLA if control is not achieved within 3 months. The driver must tell DVLA; the doctor advises, records the advice and may disclose in confidence only if he keeps driving against advice, after telling him where possible (GMC 2017).
THINK: Low testosterone, obese, sleep apnoea: treat causes first.
SAY: "Testosterone isn't safe for you now."
DO: Ask CPAP and driving; check blood count and PSA.
NUMBERS: Haematocrit above 54%: hold; PSA above 4 ng/mL: urology (Endocrine Society).
TRAP: Prescribing; letting him drive.
FINISH: Repeat levels, CPAP, DVLA, weight, review.

Bhasin S et al. Testosterone therapy in men with hypogonadism: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:1715-1744. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29562364/ Supports: Diagnosis, contraindications, monitoring and haematocrit threshold.

DVLA. Miscellaneous conditions: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025). https://www.gov.uk/guidance/miscellaneous-conditions-assessing-fitness-to-drive Supports: Obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome: moderate or severe, the driver must not drive and must notify DVLA until controlled; mild or suspected, no driving until symptoms are controlled.

GMC. Confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017). https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/confidentiality---patients-fitness-to-drive-and-reporting-concerns-to-the-dvla-or-dva Supports: advising, recording, and disclosing in confidence only if the patient keeps driving.
